cards.title: Klaviyo email system architecture: flows vs campaigns
cards.summary: Build the ecommerce email program as two layers — always-on automated flows for intent-driven moments plus a recurring campaign calendar for top-of-mind reach.
cards.use_when: Planning or auditing the overall email marketing structure for a Shopify/DTC store, deciding what should be automated versus what should be sent as one-off campaigns.
steps: Divide the program into two systems: (1) automated flows that trigger on customer behaviour (Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout, Post-Purchase) and (2) campaigns sent to segments on a schedule.
Build the automated flows first — they fire at the moments where purchase intent is highest and run without ongoing production effort.
Use campaigns on top of flows to sustain awareness and cover planned moments (promotions, launches, seasonal events).

Map each flow trigger to the customer state it serves rather than duplicating it as a campaign; flows and campaigns compete for the same inbox, so avoid sending a campaign that repeats what a flow already covers.
Review flow performance separately from campaign performance so the two systems are diagnosed with different benchmarks.
caveats: The source frames this as a Klaviyo-based architecture; the same logic applies on other ESPs but names and features differ — verify current platform capabilities.

cards.title: Set campaign cadence at 3-4 sends per week
cards.summary: The source recommends 3 to 4 email campaigns per week to stay top-of-mind without inducing list fatigue, delivered to engagement-tiered segments rather than the whole list.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns to send per week for an ecommerce list, or diagnosing why revenue from email is stalling or unsubscribes are rising.
steps: Adopt 3 to 4 campaigns per week as a starting cadence — frequent enough to keep the brand top-of-mind, restrained enough to limit fatigue.
Do not send every campaign to the entire list; route each send to engagement windows (e.g. 14/30/60/90-day active) so the most frequent sends land on the most engaged subscribers.
Track unsubscribe rate, spam complaints and open/click engagement by segment to test whether the cadence is sustainable for your list.
If engagement erodes at 4/week, reduce frequency or narrow segments rather than abandoning the cadence entirely — the problem may be relevance, not volume.
Pair high-frequency sends with clear value framing so subscribers understand why they are hearing from you.
caveats: 3-4/week is a source recommendation, not a universal benchmark; results depend on list quality, niche and content variety. Test against your own engagement data.

cards.title: Seven campaign content buckets for the email calendar
cards.summary: Fill the campaign calendar from seven recurring content categories — promotions, holidays, product launches, highlights, social proof, value/education and company updates — so high send frequency stays varied.
cards.use_when: Building a monthly or quarterly email campaign calendar for an ecommerce brand, especially when sending 3-4 times per week requires more content than promotions alone can supply.
steps: List the seven buckets: promotions, holidays, product launches, product highlights, social proof, value/education, and company updates.
Audit the last 4-8 weeks of sends and tag each one to a bucket to see which categories are over- or under-used.
For a 3-4/week cadence, rotate buckets across the month so the list is not receiving promotions for most sends.
Use social proof (reviews, UGC, press) and value/education as lower-pressure sends that maintain top-of-mind awareness between promotional pushes.
Use product launches and highlights to give existing catalogue items repeated exposure rather than only promoting new arrivals.
Reserve holidays and seasonal moments as anchors, then backfill the remaining slots with the non-promotional buckets.
caveats: Bucket weights are not prescribed by the source; the mix should be tuned to your list's tolerance and your margin structure.

cards.title: Front-load the Welcome Series into the 72-hour window
cards.summary: New subscribers convert most heavily in the first 72 hours, so the Welcome Series should front-load sends — two emails on day zero — rather than spreading content over a long drip.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding the Welcome Series flow for a store, particularly when new-subscriber revenue is concentrated in the first days after signup.
steps: Treat the first 72 hours after signup as the critical purchase window and schedule the highest-converting content there.
Send two emails on day zero — for example an immediate welcome/brand email and a second email shortly after carrying the core offer, bestsellers or social proof.
Continue the flow after day zero, but expect diminishing conversion volume as the subscriber moves further from signup.
Include a clear path to purchase (hero product, collection link, or first-purchase incentive if one is used) in the day-zero sends rather than burying it behind pure brand storytelling.
Review conversion by day-in-flow to confirm the front-loaded structure is working, and shift content earlier if later emails carry disproportionate revenue.
caveats: Two emails on day zero is the source's recommendation; sending two emails in one day can raise spam complaints if the list is low-quality or the offer is weak — monitor deliverability.

cards.title: Browse Abandonment: sell trust, not discounts
cards.summary: Browse Abandonment is a mid-funnel flow where the goal is trust-building and objection handling, not immediate discounting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or revising the Browse Abandonment flow for a store, especially when the default instinct is to lead with a coupon.
steps: Trigger the flow when a subscriber views a product (or category) without adding to cart.
Use the send to build trust and handle objections rather than offering a discount: reinforce reviews, materials, sizing, shipping/returns policy, or comparison content.
Treat the browsing subscriber as mid-funnel — they have interest but not enough conviction, so the email should reduce perceived risk.
Save discounting for later stages (cart or checkout abandonment, or a win-back) where the customer has shown stronger intent.
Test whether adding a discount at the browse stage cannibalises full-price sales from customers who would have bought anyway.
caveats: This is the source's stated approach and conflicts with common practice of discounting at every abandonment stage; if your margins or category are discount-driven, treat the no-discount rule as situational.

cards.title: Abandoned Cart and Checkout: split non-buyers from returning customers
cards.summary: Structure Abandoned Cart and Abandoned Checkout flows with explicit branches that treat non-buyers differently from returning customers.
cards.use_when: Building or optimising Abandoned Cart and Abandoned Checkout flows, or when one uniform abandonment sequence is underperforming.
steps: Build Abandoned Cart and Abandoned Checkout as separate flows — cart abandonment happens before checkout, checkout abandonment after, so intent and messaging differ.
Add a conditional split at the start of the flow that distinguishes non-buyers (never purchased) from returning customers.
For non-buyers, use the recovery emails to build trust and reduce first-purchase risk (reviews, guarantees, support contact).
For returning customers, lead with replenishment, loyalty framing or complementary products rather than first-time-buyer reassurance.
Apply incentives selectively — for example only to the non-buyer branch, or only after a defined number of emails in the sequence — rather than to every message.
Measure conversion separately for each branch so you can tell whether one split is carrying or dragging the flow.
caveats: Klaviyo's conditional-split interface changes over time; verify the current configuration steps for your account.

cards.title: Post-Purchase flow: reduce buyer's remorse and drive a 30-day repeat
cards.summary: Use the Post-Purchase sequence to reassure buyers immediately and create a second purchase within 30 days.
cards.use_when: Designing the Post-Purchase flow to lift repeat purchase rate and reduce refunds, returns or negative reviews after an order.
steps: Trigger the flow on order completion and make the first message immediate confirmation that reassures the buyer their decision was correct (order details, what happens next, brand reinforcement).
Address buyer's remorse explicitly — reinforce the purchase decision and set expectations on shipping, delivery and use.
Aim to drive a repeat purchase inside 30 days: use the flow to introduce complementary products, usage education or replenishment timing.
Sequence content so the reassurance messages come first and the cross-sell/repurchase asks come after the customer has received and used the product.
Layer in review or UGC requests at an appropriate point to build social proof that feeds back into acquisition and conversion content.
caveats: The 30-day repeat target is the source's recommendation; realistic repeat windows vary by category (consumables vs durable goods).

cards.title: Convert more site visitors with full-screen signup forms
cards.summary: Move signup form conversion from the typical 1-3% range toward 8-12% by using full-screen pop-ups and higher-commitment formats.
cards.use_when: Improving email list growth on the store's website, or when current pop-up conversion is stuck near industry-standard low single digits.
steps: Treat 1-3% as the typical baseline signup-form conversion and 8-12% as the target to test toward; use these as directional reference points, not guarantees.
Test full-screen pop-ups, which occupy the whole viewport and can outperform small corner banners by making the offer harder to ignore (while risking annoyance if mistimed).
Vary the offer and format rather than only the copy — different formats (full-page, pop-up, embedded) surface different levels of visitor intent.
Split-test desktop and mobile experiences separately, since form layout, timing and behaviour differ substantially between devices.
Monitor unsubscribe and complaint rates after raising form aggressiveness so list growth does not come at the cost of deliverability.
caveats: The 1-3% and 8-12% figures are the source's stated benchmarks, not universal results; performance depends on traffic source, offer strength and audience.

cards.title: Use micro-commitments and gamification to lift signup conversion
cards.summary: Lower the psychological cost of signing up with a two-step yes/no opener, or raise engagement with interactive formats like spin-to-win and scratch-offs.
cards.use_when: Designing or testing signup forms for a store where a single-field opt-in is converting poorly, or where traffic needs a reason to engage.
steps: Test a micro-commitment first step: an initial yes/no question (e.g. 'Want 10% off?') before asking for the email address, so the visitor commits before the larger ask.
Alternatively test gamified formats such as spin-to-win or scratch-off reveals, which give an interactive moment and a prize incentive before requesting the email.
Use these formats deliberately — they attract signups motivated by the prize, so qualify those subscribers through subsequent flows or segmentation.
Run the interactive version as a split test against the standard form so you can compare list growth against downstream engagement, not just opt-in rate.
Verify current availability of any gamification app in your ESP or app store before planning around it.
caveats: Prize-driven signups can inflate opt-ins while depressing downstream engagement; judge these formats on revenue per subscriber, not opt-in rate alone.

cards.title: Collect zero-party data with a signup quiz
cards.summary: Use a quiz as the signup form to gather declared preferences (zero-party data) that can drive segmentation and personalised flows.
cards.use_when: Building list growth and segmentation at the same time — for example when the store sells across categories and needs to know each subscriber's interests to send relevant campaigns.
steps: Design the signup quiz around answers you will actually use for segmentation: product preferences, goals, skin/hair type, experience level, or gifting context.
Keep the quiz short enough to complete — each additional question adds drop-off, so only ask what feeds a real segment or flow branch.
Route quiz answers into list properties/segments in the ESP so they can trigger different welcome content and campaign targeting.
Use the quiz answers in the Welcome Series to personalise product recommendations instead of sending the same generic bestsellers email to everyone.
Feed quiz data back into campaign planning so the seven content buckets can be assigned to the segments most likely to want them.
caveats: Quiz-based signup forms typically convert lower than a single-field email capture; the trade-off is better data and relevance, so measure downstream revenue rather than opt-in rate alone.

cards.title: Authenticate sending domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
cards.summary: Configure SPF, DKIM and DMARC so inbox providers can verify your sending domain and trust your mail.
cards.use_when: Setting up or troubleshooting email deliverability for a store, or when mail is landing in spam/promotions despite good engagement.
steps: Set up SPF records so receiving servers can confirm which IPs are authorised to send on your domain's behalf.
Enable DKIM signing so messages carry a cryptographic signature proving they were authorised by the domain owner and were not altered in transit.
Publish a DMARC policy so you receive reports on authentication failures and instruct receivers how to treat unauthenticated mail from your domain.
Work through authentication before optimising content or frequency — deliverability problems from missing authentication cannot be fixed by better subject lines.
Verify the exact DNS record values and setup steps in your current ESP and DNS host before publishing, as these interfaces change.
caveats: DNS configuration errors can break all sending from the domain; make changes with access to the DNS host and allow time for propagation.

cards.title: Clean the list: suppress subscribers inactive 180+ days
cards.summary: Protect sender reputation by regularly suppressing subscribers who have not engaged for 180 days.
cards.use_when: Routine list hygiene for an established ecommerce list, or when open rates and inbox placement are declining because of large inactive cohorts.
steps: Identify subscribers with no engagement (opens/clicks) for 180 days or more and suppress them from regular campaign sending.
Suppress rather than delete where possible, so the data is retained and can be reactivated later if needed.
Run the cleaning on a recurring schedule rather than once — inactive cohorts rebuild continuously as subscribers disengage.
Optionally run a win-back sequence before suppression to attempt reactivation, then suppress non-responders.
Track deliverability metrics before and after cleaning to confirm the suppression is improving engagement rates as expected.
caveats: 180 days is the source's benchmark; very seasonal businesses may want a longer window before suppressing otherwise-valuable seasonal buyers. Verify current suppression tooling in your ESP.

cards.title: Segment by engagement windows for primary inbox placement
cards.summary: Send to engagement-tiered segments (14/30/60/90-day active windows) so the most valuable subscribers are mailed most and poor engagement does not drag domain reputation.
cards.use_when: Setting up sending segments in the ESP, especially in AI-curated inboxes (such as Gmail's AI inbox) where engagement signals heavily influence placement.
steps: Create segments based on recency of engagement: 14-day, 30-day, 60-day and 90-day active windows.
Send your highest-frequency or highest-value campaigns to the tightest window (14-day active) so the most engaged subscribers receive the most mail.
Extend to wider windows (30/60/90-day) for lower-frequency or broader-audience sends.
Use the segments to diagnose deliverability: if 90-day-active open rates are weak, stop mailing that tier with full cadence before reputation suffers.
Combine engagement windows with the 180-day suppression rule so the least engaged subscribers exit the list rather than accumulating.
caveats: The specific window bands (14/30/60/90) are the source's heuristics; adjust to your list size and send cadence. Engagement windows reduce reach, so expect lower total sends but better inbox placement.

cards.title: A/B test flows and campaigns separately
cards.summary: Run split tests on automated flows and one-off campaigns as different testing systems, because they have different volumes and decision contexts.
cards.use_when: Setting up an email testing programme for a store, or deciding what to test next when both flows and campaigns are running.
steps: Treat flow testing and campaign testing as separate tracks with separate hypotheses — flows run continuously on triggered traffic, campaigns run on scheduled sends to segments.
For campaigns, test one variable at a time (subject line, offer, creative, send time) on comparable segments so the result is attributable.
For flows, test structural changes (branch order, delay timings, number of emails) rather than only copy, since flow performance is driven by sequence design.
Use the desktop/mobile split-test requirement for signup forms as one example: distinct experiences should be tested separately, not assumed to behave the same.
Keep a record of test outcomes so structural decisions (like day-zero email count or discount placement) are based on your own data rather than defaults.
caveats: Small lists may not reach statistical significance quickly on flow tests; extend test duration or accept directional reads rather than over-interpreting early results.

cards.title: Adapt email strategy to AI-curated inboxes
cards.summary: Gmail and other providers now sort mail with AI, so deliverability depends more on engagement signals and list hygiene than on volume.
cards.use_when: When planning sending strategy for a store whose mail increasingly lands in non-primary tabs, or when deciding whether to increase send volume.
steps: Assume the inbox provider uses engagement and behavioural signals to decide primary vs promotions placement, so poor engagement directly costs visibility.
Prioritise list hygiene (180-day suppression) and engagement-tiered segmentation over blanket list sends as the primary deliverability levers.
Keep authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) in place so AI sorting is not compounded by technical distrust.
Judge a send by its effect on engagement from the segments that matter (14/30-day active) rather than by total list reach.
Treat deliverability as an ongoing operational practice — clean and segment continuously rather than running one-off fixes.
caveats: Inbox provider behaviour and AI sorting features change frequently; verify current guidance from the provider and your ESP rather than assuming a fixed algorithm.

cards.title: Use AI analysis to interpret email marketing data
cards.summary: Apply AI tooling to analyse Klaviyo email data so you can find patterns across flows, campaigns and segments faster than manual review.
cards.use_when: When email performance data is too large to review manually — for example across many flows, segments and campaign buckets — and you need to prioritise what to fix.
steps: Feed email performance data (flow conversion, campaign engagement by segment, suppression impact) into an AI analysis workflow to surface patterns and outliers.
Use the output to generate hypotheses — for example which content bucket or flow branch underperforms — then validate with a controlled test in Klaviyo.
Do not let AI output replace the structural decisions in this system (day-zero welcome emails, browse vs cart discounting, engagement windows); use it to prioritise and diagnose.
Re-check AI-generated conclusions against the underlying segment definitions, since a mis-built segment will produce misleading analysis.
Verify current AI features and data-access options in your ESP, as these change frequently.
caveats: AI analysis is only as good as the segment and flow definitions it reads; results should be treated as hypotheses, not conclusions.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a comprehensive end-to-end Klaviyo email marketing framework for e-commerce brands, covering list growth (signup forms, micro-commitments), core automated flows (Welcome, Browse/Cart Abandonment, Post-Purchase), campaign strategy (91 campaign ideas, cadence), A/B testing protocols, list segmentation, and deliverability protection. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, Klaviyo flows, list growth, deliverability] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. email marketing / Constructing a high-performing e-commerce email marketing system. Balancing email campaign frequency (recommending 3 to 4 campaigns weekly to maintain top-of-mind awareness without inducing list fatigue) and categorizing campaign content into seven key buckets (promotions, holidays, product launches, highlights, social proof, value/education, and company updates). Klaviyo flows / Architecting core automated email sequences. Building front-loaded Welcome Series flows (deploying two emails on day zero within the critical 72-hour purchase window), Browse Abandonment sequences (focusing on mid-funnel trust and objection handling rather than immediate discounts), Abandoned Cart/Checkout flows (using strategic non-buyer vs. returning customer splits), and Post-Purchase sequences (minimizing buyer's remorse and driving repeat purchases within 30 days). list growth / Optimizing website signup forms to lift conversion rates from the 1-3% industry standard to an 8-12% target. Utilizing full-screen pop-ups, micro-commitment "yes/no" initial steps, interactive gamification (spin-to-win, scratch-offs), zero-party data collection quizzes, and split-testing distinct desktop and mobile experiences. deliverability / Maintaining inbox placement and protecting sender reputation in AI-curated email environments (like Gmail's AI inbox). Implementing technical authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), regularly cleaning unengaged subscribers (suppressing profiles inactive past 180 days), and utilizing engagement-tiered segmentation (14-day, 30-day, 60-day, and 90-day active windows) to maximize primary inbox placement.

Look for. The recommended campaign sending frequency: 3 to 4 campaigns per week. The critical purchase window for welcome flows: the first 72 hours (with day zero driving the highest conversion volume). The core Klaviyo automated flows: Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout, and Post-Purchase. The list cleaning benchmark: suppressing unengaged subscribers who have been inactive for 180 days.

Skip. Promotional pitches for the speaker's agency booking links, the free email marketing course download, or external tool affiliate links (e.g., Aaliyah, Clock Apps).

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 25 to 30.
